Of course, that’s your contention. You’re a first-year machine-learning engineer. You just got finished readin' Attention Is All You Need, probably watched a Karpathy video too. So now you’re convinced everything is just transformers and scaling laws.

That's gonna last until next month when you discover convolution, and then you're gonna be talkin' about inductive biases and locality and how CNNs were actually incredibly compute-efficient for vision.

Then you're gonna read the FlashAttention paper, and suddenly everything's about IO complexity and SRAM and how FLOPs don't matter because the whole goddamn thing is memory-bandwidth bound.

That'll last until somebody shows you an MoE model, and then you're gonna be in here regurgitating DeepSeek, talkin' about expert parallelism and active parameters and how dense models are economically obsolete.

Then six months from now you'll write one shitty Triton kernel, look at an Nsight trace for the first time, and start telling everybody Python isn't actually the bottleneck because the GPU is asynchronous.

And by next year you're gonna be standing right here explaining to me that your 400-billion-parameter model is fast because you turned on CUDA graphs.

i just automated our release and QA process!
using Grok Bot i made two Team Bots: sandcastle, my release manager, and poteto, my engineer bot. i added them to Slack and made a new channel for managing releases.

first i tell sandcastle that i want to do a cut. it'll DM all the contributors with links to their PRs so they know what goes in the next release and can DM the bot back if they have any blockers or objections.

sandcastle then kicks off the build, watches it automatically, and starts up an automated fuzz swarm. usually this is 10+ agents running on Grok 4.7 xhigh to run the build, click around and use it like a real user (using our verification skills and feature map), some are directed while a few are "chaos monkey" clicking things randomly to see what breaks. 

whenever it finds an issue, i tell it to @ mention my engineer bot poteto, to spin up a Cursor Project to own triaging and fixing all the high pri issues. depending on the severity i may ask it to cherry pick the fix into our release branch and cut a patch release, or if it's a pre-existing issue i still fix it but include in the next release instead

that's one more tedious task that Grok Bot now handles for our team

candidates.text:
Despite how much I use AI agents in my day job, the launch of dots in ChatGPT for the first time has actually changed my day-to-day life. 

Just as an example, I'm right now in Japan for a week on a work trip. I had a long 12-hour flight from LA to Osaka. The Wi-Fi wasn't all that great, so getting work done would have ordinarily been difficult.

But what I did instead was I just chatted with my Dot, told it the things that I wanted done, and got effectively a full workday out of that flight, just messaging back and forth as I simultaneously listened to podcasts and caught up on a bunch of talks I'd been meaning to review. I reviewed every side event, I prepped for every meeting. I even produced a brand new version of our sales deck, customized for every IRL conversation I was going to have. 

Then after getting to Japan, I realized I had forgotten to bring business cards. In Japanese business, exchanging business cards is very important. So I asked my Dot what to do.

It figured out that there's a bunch of 24/7 print shops in Osaka that do business cards, it translated the websites for me, created a user account, designed the business cards referencing our Airfoil brand system, and placed the order. At no point did I open the website of the business card printing company or even open Figma. It then texted me when they were ready... and I just went to the print shop and my stack of business cards were there.

The key thing here is when I'm doing design engineering or research work with AI agents, I am still very much in the driver's seat. I might hand off pieces of my work, but I'm guiding every small detail. Now that I have quite a bit of context saved and accessible for agents to use, and bluntly, agent harnesses and the underlying models themselves have just gotten so much better, being able to entirely hand off tasks and just trust that the agent will probably handle it (at least with the level of reliability of an intern) is a new feeling for me. 

At least so far, it does feel pretty liberating.

candidates.text:
Psychedelic use, for most users, is part of a cycle of persistent grief. The grandeur of the neon sea of fractals and the ability to self-smash the infinite wonder button in the brain is, in fact, a sad consolation prize for having lost the ability to make meaning of the small, mundane circumstances of life.

Wild weekend swings between the light fantastic and its faltering, depleted aftermath recapitulate the broader oscillation between narcissism and nihilsm that characterizes contemporary life. The psychedelic trip, like all psychoses, promises a revelation that never quite comes, or insinuates a transmission that is never quite  remembered. You know it's special. You know it's meaningful. It's completely, 100% yours. This time you'll find it for real. This time you'll be able to bring it back. 

"I have come to know the deepest secrets of the universe," he thinks, bleary eyed in bed at 12:30 pm on a Sunday afternoon. "I have glimpsed the mind of God" she thinks, scrolling her stories, avoiding the certain overwhelm of reading an e-mail from a once beloved college roommate.

In the meantime, dust accumulates, calls go unanswered, dinner invitations go unsent, loved ones slowly disappear from life, one mild disappointment at a time. The chores that maintain half-decency become too boring, too meaningless, too immediately unrewarding to be worth the effort. And in that thorough and terrible neglect, the desert of honesty and care at the center of postmodern subjectivity yawns. The blistering infinite sacred, on-demand, and all it costs you is your will to show up for your mundane world, to keep trying to love your frustrating family, to try something, anything to rise above the infinite guilt of your unlived life.

candidates.text:
Not sure if you noticed that our portal to Naraka in Unleash the Avatar looks similar to Balinese split gates. 

We thought a lot on how best to represent Indian hell (Naraka) and how Lord Yamraj and his subjects would behave. Most of our references were from the Rigveda and Yamagita but as we kept looking for other visual representations, we came across painted representations of Lord Yama and his servants on the ceilings of the Kerta Gosa pavilion in Bali. 

The gates in our game carry the same concept as the Balinese ones: They stand for "rwa bhineda", the balance of opposites (between worlds). While we won't use the exact real split gates in game (and our version is creative representation) to represent the 4th gate, it's still fun learning about all of the different representations of culture across the world.

I didn't want this to feel like Hell/Satan but Indian. It's overdone in games too. We wanted to do a portrayal centered on judgment, duty, and the cycle of rebirth and i think this is better grounded than a generic overlord of hell.

candidates.text:
Stop treating post-purchase confirmation emails as transaction receipts

They CAN be retention assets if you use them properly 👇

The moment immediately following a purchase is when customer excitement and brand trust are at an all time peak

Wasting that peak engagement moment on a boring system receipt is a massive missed opportunity to increase overall customer lifetime value

A strategic post purchase sequence should focus on eliminating buyer remorse reinforcing product value and driving logical repeat orders

Here is how to structure a post purchase onboarding flow that turns new buyers into loyal brand advocates over time:

1. Immediate purchase validation and excitement
- Reassure the buyer that they made a fantastic decision by choosing your brand over competitors
- Set clear expectations regarding fulfillment timelines and shipping tracking updates

2. Proactive product onboarding and usage guides
- Deliver clear step by step tutorials that help the customer get the best possible results
- Address common setup mistakes before the physical package even arrives on their doorstep

3. Community integration and social proof
- Invite new buyers to join your brand community or share unboxing videos on social media
- Highlight real customer stories to reinforce their purchase confidence

4. Timed cross sell or replenishment invite
- Introduce complementary products only after the customer has received and enjoyed their initial order
- Offer a subtle loyalty reward for placing a second order within thirty days

Optimizing your post purchase flow ensures that first time buyers have an exceptional experience from day one

When customers feel supported throughout their entire journey they naturally stay loyal and recommend your products to friends

Focusing on backend post purchase experience turns one time buyers into recurring profit drivers who fuel long term ecom growth

Most founders misread acquisition interest - particularly from strategic acquirers.

A conversation from their Corp Dev is not the same as "this company wants to acquire us right now."

They hear, "What you are building is interesting," and start doing math on the number.

In reality, these conversations are at least 6-12 months away from a number, if it ever becomes one.

Most strategic buyers (particularly larger companies) are always scouting. It's like hiring for them. Management sets the direction, and corp dev just executes it. That's why they keep in touch with bankers and email companies.

Be cautiously realistic when talking to corp dev teams. For anything to move, you have to be a really hot company in a category management is desperate to move into.

And if the acquirer isn't a large company flush with cash, assume it's going to equity at peak valuation. Then it's a 4-year vest, 1-year cliff, and they can change direction and let you go.

If it's a PE-backed company, figure out where the cash will come from. Will it come from the acquirer or their PE sponsor? Does the CEO have authority to push it through, or does the board have to approve it at the end?

As you move, you'll run into internal teams fighting for budgets and saying, "We could build this if we had the resources."

The only thing that beats the "we'll build it" argument is urgency. Someone with power needs this now. A mandate from the CEO or board. Without that, you get dragged for quarters.

Founders who get acquired well chase the highest need (even if it's not the highest number). They figure out who has the money, why they have to spend it now, and how much of that is guaranteed.
